props.title: Nostalghia

sections.content: Nostalghia (1983) represents Andrei Tarkovsky's first film made outside the Soviet Union, shot entirely in Italy with haunting precision. The film follows Russian poet Gorchakov researching a composer's life while battling profound homesickness - a mirror of Tarkovsky's own exile. Its legendary 9-minute single take of Gorchakov carrying a candle across an empty pool distills Tarkovsky's mastery of time, faith, and human endurance. Like his earlier Stalker (1979), the film transforms physical journeys into spiritual quests.

sections.content: Tarkovsky's signature long takes and metaphysical themes find kindred spirits in other European art cinema giants. Theo Angelopoulos's Ulysses' Gaze (1995) shares Nostalghia's preoccupation with exile and cultural memory. Béla Tarr's Werckmeister Harmonies (2000) similarly uses extended sequences and stark landscapes to explore faith and despair. These films reject conventional plotting for atmospheric immersion and philosophical weight. SUBHEAD: The Cinema of Exile and Memory

The themes of displacement and nostalgia in Nostalghia resonate through later works like Atom Egoyan's Calendar (1993) and Andrey Zvyagintsev's The Return (2003). Both films grapple with cultural identity and separation from homeland. The meditative pace and rich symbolism of The Great Beauty (2013) by Paolo Sorrentino shows Tarkovsky's enduring influence on contemporary European cinema, especially in its treatment of time and memory as malleable substances.
